notes: Leading authority on mistake of law and litigation compromises after Kleinwort Benson; Court of Appeal allowed Islington's appeal.

enrichment.short_title: Compromise vitiated by mistake of law after CPR service dispute
key_facts: Miss Brennan issued proceedings against Islington and two solicitor firms for carbon monoxide injuries but the claim form was struck out for late service under Godwin and Anderton.
Her solicitor agreed with Islington's solicitor to discontinue the Islington action on a no-costs basis, believing the strike-out was valid.
The Court of Appeal later reversed Anderton, vindicating Brennan's service argument, but Islington sought to hold her to the discontinuance agreement.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Second-tier appeal on whether a consent discontinuance based on a shared mistake of law as to CPR service timing could be set aside.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; the compromise was not vitiated by mistake of law and Islington could rely on the discontinuance agreement.
enrichment.ratio: A compromise of extant litigation entered on professional advice in a state of legal doubt rather than clear mistake, without inquiry about pending appeals, and where performance remained possible, should not be set aside for retrospective change in the law; the risk of subsequent judicial decisions is impliedly accepted in litigation compromises.
legal_issues: Whether Kleinwort Benson extends to vitiating compromises by mistake of law
Whether the parties shared a mistake or merely doubt about CPR service timing
Application of The Great Peace impossibility test to compromises
Public policy protecting finality of litigation settlements

notes: Animal welfare judicial review on broiler breeder feed restriction; dismissal and proportionality analysis are clear.

enrichment.short_title: Broiler breeder feed restriction welfare challenge dismissed
key_facts: Compassion in World Farming challenged DEFRA's policy of not prosecuting owners who restrict feeding of broiler breeder chickens to control weight and improve breeding performance.
Restricted feeding during the first 20 weeks causes persistent hunger but avoids obesity-related mortality and reproductive failure in fast-growing genotypes.
Newman J dismissed the judicial review; the claimants sought declarations that the feeding regime breached welfare regulations.
The claimants did not seek ad libitum feeding, which the evidence showed would harm bird health.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from judicial review refusing mandatory prosecution and declarations on broiler breeder feed restriction policy.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; restricted feeding compatible with paragraph 22 of Schedule 1 when owners take all reasonable steps to promote composite well-being.
enrichment.ratio: Well-being under the farm welfare regulations is a composite state requiring balance of conflicting welfare factors; where a wholesome diet maintains health and satisfies nutritional needs, persistent hunger during immaturity does not alone establish breach of the duty to promote positive well-being, and the court cannot order prosecution on general evidence without proof of routine contravention.
legal_issues: Meaning of 'promote a positive state of well-being' in Schedule 1 paragraph 22
Whether chronic hunger in broiler breeders requires prosecution
Whether commercial interests may be balanced against animal welfare in enforcement
Whether slower-growing genotypes must be mandated through welfare regulations
linked_authorities: R (on the application of Compassion in World Farming Ltd) v Secretary of State [2003] EWHC 2850 (Admin)

confidence.notes: Appeal outcome and construction of paragraph 22 are clearly articulated by May LJ.

notes: Section 68 serious irregularity in ICC bribery arbitration; remittal on fair value quantification is clearly ordered.

enrichment.short_title: Arbitration award remitted over undisclosed valuation approach
key_facts: Camair claimed rescission and restitution of about US$55.5m paid under aircraft maintenance contracts tainted by bribery through agent ATT.

The ICC tribunal unanimously held Camair must tender value received but the majority valued services at Transnet's commercial price less commission rather than cost-based quantification argued by both parties.
The parties' evidence and closing submissions focused on Transnet's costs using maintenance cost forecasts and a 15% profit margin.
Camair's nominated arbitrator dissented on both the valuation methodology and commission calculation.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Commercial Court challenge under section 68 Arbitration Act 1996 to set aside or remit a final ICC arbitral award.
enrichment.outcome: Serious irregularity established on fair value quantification; award remitted to the tribunal for reconsideration of the value of maintenance services; commission award upheld.
enrichment.ratio: Where an arbitral tribunal decides quantum on a valuation basis neither party advanced, without warning or opportunity to address it, despite both parties proceeding on a shared cost-based approach, the tribunal fails section 33 fairness requirements and section 68 substantial injustice is likely on remittal.
legal_issues: Whether the tribunal departed from the parties' agreed quantification approach without fair notice
Meaning of value to Camair versus cost to Transnet under South African restitution law
Whether use of document R1 on commission involved procedural unfairness
Scope of section 68 serious irregularity and substantial injustice

notes: Unusual race discrimination case where objective justification defence was struck out; pay detriment finding reversed on appeal.

enrichment.short_title: Indirect race pay discrimination at Spanish school in London
key_facts: Mr Spicer, a British teacher at the Colegio Español Vicente Cañada Blanch in London, claimed indirect race discrimination in pay compared with seconded Spanish civil servants.
Spanish civil servants received lower basic salaries but substantial relocation allowances producing higher total packages than locally recruited British teachers.
The employment tribunal struck out Spain's objective justification defence for failure to comply with a directions order.
The tribunal nonetheless held there was no pay detriment because Mr Spicer's basic salary exceeded that of Spanish civil servants.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the Court of Appeal on indirect race discrimination in pay after Employment Appeal Tribunal partial dismissal.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed on pay; matter remitted for compensation assessment rather than full rehearing.
enrichment.ratio: Where a requirement to be a Spanish civil servant seconded from Spain to receive relocation allowances has disproportionate impact on British staff and the employer cannot rely on objective justification because that defence was struck out, paying a British teacher substantially less overall for the same work is a detriment; section 3(4) is satisfied by comparing all teachers at the school.
legal_issues: Identification of the requirement or condition for indirect discrimination purposes
Meaning of detriment where basic pay differs from total pay package
Effect of striking out objective justification on the discrimination analysis
Application of section 3(4) like-for-like comparison to the relevant pool

notes: VAT tour operators margin scheme after ECJ reference; Marleasing read-down of domestic leaflet is clearly explained.

enrichment.short_title: VAT margin scheme includes agent top-up on discounted holidays
key_facts: First Choice sold package holidays through agents permitted to discount below brochure price if the agent paid the shortfall to First Choice.
Customers paid the discounted price while First Choice invoiced and accounted for the full brochure price including the agent's top-up.
First Choice claimed VAT repayment on the basis that taxable margin should be calculated on the lower customer price only.
The ECJ held the agent's additional payment formed part of the total amount to be paid by the traveller under Article 26(2).
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal after ECJ preliminary ruling on whether domestic VAT guidance could be construed consistently with EU law.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed for Customs and Excise; domestic VAT leaflet read purposively to include agent top-ups in the selling price.
enrichment.ratio: Following an ECJ ruling that third-party consideration linked to the holiday supply forms part of the traveller's total payment under Article 26(2), the Marleasing principle requires the domestic tour operators margin scheme, including VAT leaflet wording on total charge to customers, to be construed compatibly as covering payments made for the traveller's benefit.
legal_issues: Whether agent discounts reduce the tour operator's taxable margin
Characterisation of agent top-up payments under Article 26(2)
Marleasing and Litster-style interpretation of domestic tax guidance
Legal certainty in VAT legislation

notes: Important section 44 stop-and-search principles upheld but operational fairness concerns and thin police evidence limit confidence in individual stop outcomes.

enrichment.short_title: Section 44 terrorism stop and search at arms fair protest
key_facts: Kevin Gillan and Pennie Quinton were stopped and searched near the DSEi arms fair in London under rolling section 44 authorisations for the whole Metropolitan Police District.
The authorisations had been renewed every 28 days since 2001 and confirmed by the Secretary of State without public announcement.
Police evidence on briefing and instructions given to officers at the protest was described as lamentably inadequate.
The Divisional Court dismissed the claims; Liberty appealed on statutory construction, proportionality and legality grounds.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from judicial review of lawfulness of section 44 authorisations and stop-and-search at an arms fair protest.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed on authorisation and confirmation issues; court expressed concern about police evidence on operational use but made no final remedial order.
enrichment.ratio: Section 44 permits random stop and search without reasonable suspicion when a senior officer considers it expedient for preventing terrorism and the Secretary of State confirms the authorisation; rolling London-wide authorisations may be lawful in the current terrorist context, but interference must be for the statutory purpose and proportionate, and the police must demonstrate fair operational use.
legal_issues: Construction of 'expedient' in section 44(3)
Lawfulness of rolling Metropolitan-wide authorisations
Whether stop and search engaged Articles 5, 8, 10 and 11 ECHR
Whether powers were used for protest policing rather than terrorism prevention

confidence.notes: Statutory and authorisation holdings are clear, but individual stop lawfulness was not finally resolved on thin evidence.

notes: Extradition habeas corpus on delay under section 11(3)(b); Kakis principles applied clearly to refuse discharge.

enrichment.short_title: Extradition habeas corpus refused despite seven-year delay
key_facts: Darren Sapstead was sought by Spain for negligent manslaughter after Garry Walton drowned on a Tenerife pleasure cruise in November 1996.
Prosecution relied on later statements from Katie and Lucy Smethurst alleging Sapstead deliberately threw Walton overboard.
Sapstead returned to the UK the day after the incident and was not arrested until January 2004, about seven years after the Smethurst accounts changed.
He was committed at Bow Street and applied for habeas corpus on passage-of-time grounds.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Habeas corpus application challenging return to Spain after committal under the Extradition Act 1989.
enrichment.outcome: Application refused; return to Spain held neither unjust nor oppressive despite inexcusable delay.
enrichment.ratio: Under section 11(3)(b) unjust return relates primarily to trial prejudice and oppressive return to hardship from changed circumstances; long delay does not render extradition unjust where a grave offence has a strong prima facie case, witness memories concern a stark dramatic event unlikely to fade, and the applicant's subsequent marriage and employment do not make return oppressive.
legal_issues: Whether seven-year delay made extradition unjust or oppressive
Effect of changed witness statements on fairness of trial
Whether other cruise witnesses could no longer be traced
Application of Kakis v Cyprus to delay not caused by the accused

notes: Part 8 pension scheme construction on deficit powers and money purchase status; detailed declarations clearly given.

enrichment.short_title: KPMG pension scheme deficit and money purchase status
key_facts: The KPMG Staff Pension Scheme Pre-2000 Fund showed a deficit rising to about £71m on the 2002 actuarial valuation.
The trustee sought court directions on whether it could reduce pensions in payment under clause 8.5 and whether the scheme was a money purchase scheme.
Benefits were calculated by applying age and sex factors to annual contributions rather than by final salary formula alone.
KPMG argued money purchase status excluded minimum funding and section 75 employer debt obligations.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Part 8 Pension Schemes Act 1995 application for declarations on trustee powers and scheme classification.
enrichment.outcome: Declarations that clause 8.5 includes power to reduce pensions in payment subject to section 67; scheme held not a money purchase scheme; question 4 did not arise.
enrichment.ratio: Clause 8.5 empowers trustees with employer consent to adjust benefits including pensions in payment to restore solvency, but exercise reducing accrued entitlements engages section 67; a scheme providing average-salary-weighted defined benefits and discretionary bonuses is not a money purchase scheme even where contributions are multiplied by actuarial factors.
legal_issues: Whether clause 8.5 extends to reductions in pensions already in payment
Whether exercise of clause 8.5 is a modification under section 67
Whether the KPMG scheme is a money purchase scheme
Meaning of money purchase benefits versus average salary benefits
linked_authorities: Stevens v Bell [2002] PLR 247
Barclays Bank plc v Holmes [2000] PLR 339

confidence.notes: Declarations on questions 1 to 3 are explicit; question 5 was adjourned.

notes: Disability discrimination strike-out on section 6 selection criteria; permission refused following Thompsons.

enrichment.short_title: Disability adjustment of job criteria claim struck out
key_facts: Mr Bruce, a wheelchair-user solicitor, applied for an employment law post with Kennedys but was rejected for lacking TUPE and corporate employment experience.
He had previously failed in Bruce v Cavalier and Thompsons on a similar section 6 argument that selection criteria should be adjusted for disability.
The employment tribunal chairman struck out the section 5(2)/6 reasonable adjustment claim as misconceived but allowed section 5(1) and victimisation claims to proceed.
The EAT upheld the strike-out; Bruce renewed permission to appeal to the Court of Appeal.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Renewed application for permission to appeal from EAT decision upholding partial strike-out of disability discrimination claim.
enrichment.outcome: Permission to appeal refused; no reasonable prospect of success on section 6 adjustment of selection criteria argument.
enrichment.ratio: Where selection criteria unrelated to disability, such as knowledge of TUPE, disqualify a disabled applicant equally capable of meeting them as a non-disabled applicant, no section 6 duty arises to adjust the criteria; Thompsons remains binding and such a claim may be struck out as misconceived.
legal_issues: Whether section 6 requires adjustment of selection criteria unrelated to disability
Need for causal connection between disability and substantial disadvantage
Binding effect of Bruce v Thompsons on subsequent employment claims
When discrimination claims may be struck out as misconceived

notes: Polkey/O'Dea/King v Eaton analysis on redundancy consultation; pension issue remitted for inadequate Meek reasons.

enrichment.short_title: Unfair redundancy: Polkey reduction and pension misdirection
key_facts: Mr Lambe, a corporate finance manager at telecoms company 186K, was made redundant after refusing transfer to financial control when Ian Perry took his role.
The tribunal found genuine redundancy but procedural unfairness for inadequate consultation, limiting compensation to seven weeks plus statutory rights.
The tribunal rejected a pension-loss claim relating to pay-in-lieu of notice versus working notice to reach two-year scheme vesting.
The EAT dismissed the appeal at a preliminary hearing; the Court of Appeal heard the full appeal after permission.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from Employment Appeal Tribunal dismissal of unfair-dismissal appeal, including Polkey compensation and pension directions.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed on redundancy and Polkey issues; allowed in part to remit pension compensation issue to the employment tribunal.
enrichment.ratio: On redundancy facts found by the tribunal, a Polkey reduction was permissible: extended consultation would not have retained the employee; procedural/substantive labels are unhelpful under O'Dea; failure to identify and address the pension issue was an error of law warranting remission under ERA 1996 section 123(1).
legal_issues: Whether dismissal was by reason of redundancy under section 139
Polkey reduction after unfair consultation
Procedural versus substantive unfairness in redundancy selection
Loss of deferred pension attributable to unfair dismissal
